scope: Scientific manifest/DAG execution with pinned Linux SeqKit and VSEARCH releases and MUSCLE workbench1 source build; native Windows inventory and declared asset hashes checked before execution. Eight additional unit tests isolate self-check runner behavior with a copy backend.

executedGraphs.name: Dereplicate and cluster amplicon reads
executedGraphs.methods:
Executed methods (only successfully completed operations are described):

Step S1 (FASTQ to nucleotide FASTA) was performed using seqkit 2.14.0 (pack seqkit 0.5.2). FASTQ records were converted to nucleotide FASTA using SeqKit fq2fa, discarding per-base quality scores. Settings: Threads=1. Inputs: Fastq reads: I1 · Six unpaired amplicon reads.

Step S4 (Original amplicon read statistics) was performed using seqkit 2.14.0 (pack seqkit 0.5.2). FASTQ records were validated with SeqKit seq before analysis. Sequence statistics were calculated with SeqKit stats using all-statistics tabular output; FASTQ quality encoding was Phred+33. Settings: Threads=1. Inputs: Fastq reads: I1 · Six unpaired amplicon reads.

Step S2 (Count unique amplicons) was performed using vsearch 2.32.0 (pack vsearch 0.5.2). Full-length nucleotide sequences were dereplicated using VSEARCH fastx_uniques with the configured strand comparison. Each input record contributed one count; prior header abundance values were not used. Unique sequences were sorted by abundance and written with new Uniq identifiers and explicit size annotations (--sizeout); UC membership was retained. Settings: Strand comparison=plus. Inputs: Nucleotide sequences: S1 · FASTQ to nucleotide FASTA → FASTQ to nucleotide FASTA output.

Step S3 (Cluster at 97 percent identity) was performed using vsearch 2.32.0 (pack vsearch 0.5.2). Abundance-annotated sequences were greedily clustered with VSEARCH cluster_size in decreasing abundance order using the configured identity threshold and strand policy. Identity used matching columns divided by alignment length excluding terminal gaps (iddef 2); nucleotide masking was disabled. The heuristic centroid search used maxaccepts 1 and maxrejects 32. Input abundances were summed into OTU centroid size annotations; this produces OTU-style clusters, not ASVs. Settings: Minimum global identity=0.97; Strand comparison=plus; Threads=1. Inputs: Sequences with abundance labels: S2 · Count unique amplicons → Unique sequences with abundances.

Step S5 (Combine statistics reports) was performed using Combine statistics reports (pack builtin 0.5.0). Collect selected statistics into a local HTML report with a separate, attributed section for each input. Counts are not pooled and variant files are not merged. Settings: Report title=Amplicon operation evidence. Inputs: Statistics to include: S2 · Count unique amplicons → VSEARCH run statistics; S3 · Cluster at 97 percent identity → VSEARCH run statistics; S4 · Original amplicon read statistics → Statistics: FASTQ reads output.

Tool references:
Shen W, Sipos B, Zhao L. SeqKit2: A Swiss Army Knife for Sequence and Alignment Processing. iMeta (2024), e191. https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.191
Rognes et al. (2016). VSEARCH: a versatile open source tool for metagenomics. PeerJ 4:e2584. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.2584

Operations run locally in dependency order. Independent branches are scheduled sequentially. The run record records exact packs, parameters, input identities, outputs and completion states.

executedGraphs.name: Filter and align RNA without changing uracil
executedGraphs.methods:
Executed methods (only successfully completed operations are described):

Step S1 (Length filter: nucleotide FASTA) was performed using seqkit 2.14.0 (pack seqkit 0.5.2). Sequences were filtered by inclusive record length using SeqKit seq with alphabet validation. Settings: Minimum length=1; Maximum length=1000000000; Threads=1. Inputs: Nucleotide fasta: I1 · Sequences.

Step S2 (Align nucleotide sequences) was performed using muscle 5.3-workbench1 (pack muscle 0.5.2). Homologous nucleotide sequences were aligned with MUSCLE 5.3-workbench1 using the standard -align algorithm and an explicitly selected nucleotide alphabet. One alignment replicate was produced; the recorded thread count, perturbation seed and guide-tree permutation define its settings. Settings: CPU threads=1; Perturbation seed=0; Guide-tree permutation=none. Inputs: Unaligned nucleotide sequences: S1 · Length filter: nucleotide FASTA → Length filter: nucleotide FASTA output.

Tool references:
Shen W, Sipos B, Zhao L. SeqKit2: A Swiss Army Knife for Sequence and Alignment Processing. iMeta (2024), e191. https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.191
Edgar RC (2022). High-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased assessments of sequence homology and phylogeny. Nature Communications 13, 6968. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-34630-w

executedGraphs.name: Translate and align protein
executedGraphs.methods:
Executed methods (only successfully completed operations are described):

Step S1 (Translate nucleotide FASTA) was performed using seqkit 2.14.0 (pack seqkit 0.5.2). Nucleotide FASTA sequences were translated with SeqKit translate using the specified reading frame and genetic code, retaining stop codons and appending frame identifiers. Settings: Reading frame=1; Genetic code=1; Threads=1. Inputs: Nucleotide fasta: I1 · Sequences.

Step S2 (Align protein sequences) was performed using muscle 5.3-workbench1 (pack muscle 0.5.2). executedGraphs.name: Preserve weighted observations
executedGraphs.methods:
Executed methods (only successfully completed operations are described):

Step S1 (VSEARCH: dereplicate abundance sequences) was performed using vsearch 2.32.0 (pack vsearch 0.5.2). Full-length nucleotide sequences were dereplicated using VSEARCH fastx_uniques with the configured strand comparison. Existing positive size annotations were summed (--sizein). Unique sequences were sorted by abundance and written with new Uniq identifiers and explicit size annotations (--sizeout); UC membership was retained. Settings: Strand comparison=plus. Inputs: Sequences with abundance labels: I1 · Sequences.

Step S2 (VSEARCH: filter sequence abundance) was performed using vsearch 2.32.0 (pack vsearch 0.5.2). Sequences were filtered by their positive size annotations using VSEARCH sortbysize and the configured minimum abundance. Retained sequences were sorted by decreasing abundance without changing their counts. This threshold is not an error-model denoising step. Settings: Minimum abundance=3. Inputs: Sequences with abundance labels: S1 · VSEARCH: dereplicate abundance sequences → Unique sequences with abundances.

Tool references:
Rognes et al. (2016). VSEARCH: a versatile open source tool for metagenomics. PeerJ 4:e2584. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.2584
